subtopic: Types of vectors: zero, unit, equal, collinear, coinitial
concept_tested: Definition of coinitial vectors
stem: Two or more vectors are said to be coinitial if

options.A: they have the same terminal point
options.C: they lie along the same line or along parallel lines
options.D: they have the same initial point

correct_answer_text: they have the same initial point

distractor_rationale.A: The student swaps the initial point for the terminal point in the definition.
distractor_rationale.B: The student confuses coinitial vectors with vectors of equal magnitude.
distractor_rationale.C: The student gives the definition of collinear vectors instead of coinitial vectors.

solution: By definition, a vector is fixed by its initial point, its magnitude and its direction. Vectors drawn from one and the same starting point are called coinitial, so for example $\overrightarrow{OA}$, $\overrightarrow{OB}$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}$ are coinitial because each of them starts at O. Their magnitudes and directions may be completely different. Vectors having the same terminal point are called coterminal, which is a different idea, and vectors along the same or parallel lines are called collinear. Hence the defining feature of coinitial vectors is the common initial point.
formula_principle: Vectors having the same initial point are called coinitial vectors. Vectors along the same line or along parallel lines are called collinear vectors.
common_misconception: The student mixes up the common initial point with a common terminal point, or with equality of magnitude.

subtopic: Types of vectors: zero, unit, equal, collinear, coinitial
concept_tested: Recognising collinear vectors from a scalar multiple with a negative scalar
stem: If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = -6\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}$, then the two vectors are

options.C: equal in magnitude and in direction

distractor_rationale.A: The student notices that one vector is a scalar multiple of the other but ignores the negative sign of that scalar.
distractor_rationale.C: The student reads the same pattern of components and calls the two vectors equal.
distractor_rationale.D: The student believes collinear vectors must have identical components.

solution: Compare the components. Dividing each component of $\vec{b}$ by the corresponding component of $\vec{a}$ gives $\dfrac{-6}{2} = -3$, $\dfrac{3}{-1} = -3$ and $\dfrac{-6}{2} = -3$. The three ratios are equal, so $\vec{b} = -3\vec{a}$ and the vectors are collinear. The scalar $-3$ is negative, so $\vec{b}$ points in the direction opposite to $\vec{a}$. Their magnitudes are $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$ and $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{36 + 9 + 36} = 9 = 3|\vec{a}|$, so they are certainly not equal vectors.
formula_principle: $\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ if $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda \ne 0$. The two vectors are similarly directed when $\lambda > 0$ and oppositely directed when $\lambda < 0$.
common_misconception: The student treats any scalar multiple as giving the same direction, ignoring the sign of the scalar.

subtopic: Types of vectors: zero, unit, equal, collinear, coinitial
concept_tested: Equal magnitudes together with collinearity do not force equality of vectors
stem: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be non-zero collinear vectors with $|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}|$. Then

distractor_rationale.A: The student assumes that equal magnitudes along one line force the same direction.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes that two distinct symbols must stand for oppositely directed vectors.
distractor_rationale.D: The student remembers only the anti-parallel case and states it as the general conclusion.

solution: Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are collinear and $\vec{a} \ne \vec{0}$, write $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda$. Taking magnitudes, $|\vec{b}| = |\lambda|\,|\vec{a}|$. The data give $|\vec{b}| = |\vec{a}| \ne 0$, hence $|\lambda| = 1$, so $\lambda = 1$ or $\lambda = -1$. Therefore $\vec{b} = \vec{a}$ or $\vec{b} = -\vec{a}$, and both cases genuinely occur. For instance $\vec{a} = \hat{i}$ with $\vec{b} = \hat{i}$ satisfies the data, and so does $\vec{a} = \hat{i}$ with $\vec{b} = -\hat{i}$. So neither single case can be asserted for every pair.
formula_principle: If $\vec{b}$ is collinear with $\vec{a}$ then $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$, and taking magnitudes gives $|\vec{b}| = |\lambda||\vec{a}|$.
common_misconception: The student concludes one of the two cases only, forgetting that $|\lambda| = 1$ has two solutions.

subtopic: Magnitude of a vector
concept_tested: Magnitude of a vector given in component form
stem: If $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$, then $|\vec{a}|$ =

distractor_rationale.B: The student stops at the sum of the squares and omits the square root.
distractor_rationale.C: The student adds the absolute values of the three components.
distractor_rationale.D: The student uses only the $\hat{i}$ and $\hat{j}$ components and drops the $\hat{k}$ component.

solution: Here $a_{1} = 3$, $a_{2} = -4$ and $a_{3} = 12$. Then $a_{1}^{2} + a_{2}^{2} + a_{3}^{2} = 9 + 16 + 144 = 169$. The magnitude is the square root of this sum, so $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{169} = 13$. Note that squaring removes the sign of $-4$, so the negative component contributes $16$, not $-16$, and the square root at the end is essential because $169$ is the square of the length, not the length.
common_misconception: The student reports the sum of the squares as the magnitude, forgetting the square root.

subtopic: Magnitude of a vector
concept_tested: Finding an unknown component from a given magnitude
stem: If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + p\hat{k}$ with $p > 0$ and $|\vec{a}| = 7$, then $p$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student solves correctly up to $p^{2} = 36$ and reports $p^{2}$ as the answer.
distractor_rationale.B: The student writes $2 + 3 + p = 7$, adding components instead of squares.
distractor_rationale.D: The student adds $49$ and $13$ instead of subtracting $13$ from $49$.

solution: From $|\vec{a}| = 7$, squaring gives $2^{2} + 3^{2} + p^{2} = 7^{2}$, that is $4 + 9 + p^{2} = 49$. Hence $p^{2} = 49 - 13 = 36$, so $p = \pm 6$. The condition $p > 0$ selects $p = 6$. A check confirms the value, since $\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. The two traps here are stopping at $p^{2} = 36$, and squaring only the magnitude while adding the components on the left.
common_misconception: The student reports $p^{2}$ instead of $p$, or adds the components instead of their squares.

subtopic: Magnitude of a vector
concept_tested: Magnitude of a linear combination is not the same combination of magnitudes
stem: If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, then $|2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}|$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student computes $2|\vec{a}| - 3|\vec{b}| = 14 - 9$, distributing the magnitude over the combination.
distractor_rationale.B: The student computes $2|\vec{a}| + 3|\vec{b}| = 14 + 9$, adding the two magnitudes.
distractor_rationale.D: The student forms the correct vector but omits the square root at the last step.

solution: First form the vector. $2\vec{a} = 4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$ and $3\vec{b} = 6\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$, so $2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b} = (4 - 6)\hat{i} + (6 + 3)\hat{j} + (12 - 6)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} + 9\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{(-2)^{2} + 9^{2} + 6^{2}} = \sqrt{4 + 81 + 36} = \sqrt{121} = 11$. Observe that $|\vec{a}| = 7$ and $|\vec{b}| = 3$, so $2|\vec{a}| - 3|\vec{b}| = 5$, which is not the answer. Magnitude is not a linear operation, so the components must be combined first.
formula_principle: First combine componentwise, $2\vec{a} - 3\vec{b}$, and only then take the magnitude. In general $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| \ne |\vec{a}| + |\vec{b}|$.
common_misconception: The student applies the magnitude to each term separately instead of combining the vectors first.

subtopic: Unit vector in the direction of a given vector
concept_tested: Forming the unit vector along a given vector
stem: The unit vector in the direction of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student divides by $|\vec{a}|^{2}$ instead of $|\vec{a}|$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the sum of the components instead of by the magnitude.
distractor_rationale.D: The student takes a further square root and divides by $\sqrt{|\vec{a}|}$.

solution: First find the magnitude. $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2^{2} + 3^{2} + 6^{2}} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. Then divide the vector itself by this number, giving $\hat{a} = \dfrac{2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}}{7} = \dfrac{2}{7}\hat{i} + \dfrac{3}{7}\hat{j} + \dfrac{6}{7}\hat{k}$. A check is worthwhile, since $\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{2}{7}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{3}{7}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{6}{7}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36}}{7} = \dfrac{7}{7} = 1$, so the vector obtained really has unit length.
formula_principle: The unit vector along $\vec{a}$ is $\hat{a} = \dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$, provided $\vec{a} \ne \vec{0}$.
common_misconception: The student divides by the square of the magnitude, or by the sum of the components, instead of by the magnitude.

subtopic: Unit vector in the direction of a given vector
concept_tested: Unit vector along the vector joining two given points
stem: If A and B have position vectors $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 15\hat{k}$, the unit vector in the direction of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student computes the position vector of A minus that of B, reversing the vector joining the two points.
distractor_rationale.B: The student divides by the square of the magnitude.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the sum of the components instead of by the magnitude.

solution: The vector joining A to B is the position vector of the terminal point minus that of the initial point, so $\overrightarrow{AB} = \left(4\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 15\hat{k}\right) - \left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}\right) = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$. Its magnitude is $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{9 + 16 + 144} = \sqrt{169} = 13$. Hence the unit vector along $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $\dfrac{1}{13}\left(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}\right)$. Had the subtraction been taken the other way round the answer would have been the unit vector along $\overrightarrow{BA}$, which points the opposite way.
formula_principle: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$, where $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are the position vectors of A and B, and the required unit vector is $\dfrac{\overrightarrow{AB}}{|\overrightarrow{AB}|}$.
common_misconception: The student subtracts in the wrong order and produces the unit vector along $\overrightarrow{BA}$.

subtopic: Unit vector in the direction of a given vector
concept_tested: Constructing a vector of a stated magnitude in a given direction
stem: The vector of magnitude $21$ in the direction of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student multiplies the given vector by $21$ without first dividing by its magnitude.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the square of the magnitude before scaling.
distractor_rationale.D: The student stops at the unit vector and forgets to scale it up to the required magnitude.

solution: First compute $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{2^{2} + (-3)^{2} + 6^{2}} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$. The unit vector along $\vec{a}$ is therefore $\dfrac{1}{7}\left(2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right)$. Multiplying it by the required magnitude $21$ gives $\dfrac{21}{7}\left(2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right) = 3\left(2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right) = 6\hat{i} - 9\hat{j} + 18\hat{k}$. Checking, $\sqrt{36 + 81 + 324} = \sqrt{441} = 21$, as required, and the vector is a positive multiple of $\vec{a}$, so its direction is unchanged.
formula_principle: A vector of magnitude $k$ in the direction of $\vec{a}$ is $k\hat{a} = k\dfrac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$.
common_misconception: The student scales the given vector directly by the required magnitude without normalising it first.

subtopic: Unit vector in the direction of a given vector
concept_tested: Unit vector opposite to a scalar multiple of the vector joining two points
stem: If A is $(3, 1, -2)$ and B is $(1, -2, 4)$, the unit vector in the direction opposite to $2\overrightarrow{AB}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student normalises $2\overrightarrow{AB}$ but keeps its own direction instead of the opposite one.
distractor_rationale.B: The student divides $2\overrightarrow{AB}$ by $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ instead of by $|2\overrightarrow{AB}|$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides by the magnitude of the wrong vector and also keeps the original direction.

solution: First, $\overrightarrow{AB} = (1 - 3)\hat{i} + (-2 - 1)\hat{j} + (4 + 2)\hat{k} = -2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$, so $|\overrightarrow{AB}| = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$. Then $2\overrightarrow{AB} = -4\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$ and $|2\overrightarrow{AB}| = 2 \times 7 = 14$. The unit vector along $2\overrightarrow{AB}$ is $\dfrac{-4\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}}{14} = \dfrac{1}{7}\left(-2\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right)$, and the unit vector in the opposite direction is its negative, $\dfrac{1}{7}\left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 6\hat{k}\right)$. Note that doubling a vector does not change its unit vector, so the factor $2$ only matters if the magnitude used for division is also doubled.
formula_principle: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$; a unit vector opposite to a vector $\vec{v}$ is $-\dfrac{\vec{v}}{|\vec{v}|}$, and $|k\vec{v}| = |k||\vec{v}|$.
common_misconception: The student divides by the magnitude of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ rather than of $2\overrightarrow{AB}$, so the result is not of unit length.

subtopic: Addition and subtraction of vectors in component form
concept_tested: Adding two vectors given in component form
stem: If $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 4\hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ =

distractor_rationale.B: The student subtracts the second vector from the first instead of adding.
distractor_rationale.C: The student subtracts the first vector from the second.
distractor_rationale.D: The student ignores the minus sign on the $\hat{j}$ component of the first vector.

solution: Add the coefficients of $\hat{i}$, of $\hat{j}$ and of $\hat{k}$ separately. For $\hat{i}$, $3 + 2 = 5$. For $\hat{j}$, $-2 + 1 = -1$. For $\hat{k}$, $1 + (-4) = -3$. Hence $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. The signs must be carried through the addition; adding $-2$ and $1$ gives $-1$, not $3$.
formula_principle: Vectors in component form are added componentwise: $(a_{1} + b_{1})\hat{i} + (a_{2} + b_{2})\hat{j} + (a_{3} + b_{3})\hat{k}$.
common_misconception: The student mishandles the signs of the components, or subtracts when addition is asked for.

subtopic: Addition and subtraction of vectors in component form
concept_tested: Recovering a vector from the sum and the difference of two vectors
stem: If $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{a} - \vec{b} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, then $\vec{a}$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student halves the difference of the two given vectors and so obtains $\vec{b}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student adds the two given vectors but forgets to halve the result.
distractor_rationale.D: The student subtracts the two given vectors and forgets to halve the result.

solution: Add the two given vectors. $(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + (\vec{a} - \vec{b}) = 2\vec{a}$, and on the right, $\left(5\hat{i} + \hat{j}\right) + \left(\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}\right) = 6\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$. Hence $2\vec{a} = 6\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$, so $\vec{a} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$. As a check, subtracting instead gives $2\vec{b} = 4\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, so $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}$, and indeed $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = 5\hat{i} + \hat{j}$, matching the data. Note that the $\hat{k}$ component of the first datum is $0$.
formula_principle: Adding the two given equations gives $2\vec{a}$, so $\vec{a} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left[(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) + (\vec{a} - \vec{b})\right]$.
common_misconception: The student forgets the factor one half, or solves for the other vector by mistake.

subtopic: Addition and subtraction of vectors in component form
concept_tested: Triangle law applied to two sides of a triangle in component form
stem: In triangle ABC, $\overrightarrow{AB} = 3\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \hat{i} + 4\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$. Then $\overrightarrow{AC}$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $\overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{AB} - \overrightarrow{BC}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student writes $\overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{BC} - \overrightarrow{AB}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student computes $\overrightarrow{CA}$ and reports it as $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

solution: The terminal point of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is the initial point of $\overrightarrow{BC}$, so the triangle law applies directly and $\overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC}$. Adding componentwise, the $\hat{i}$ component is $3 + 1 = 4$, the $\hat{j}$ component is $-1 + 4 = 3$ and the $\hat{k}$ component is $2 + (-5) = -3$. Hence $\overrightarrow{AC} = 4\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$. The reversed vector $\overrightarrow{CA}$ is the negative of this, so the order of the letters must be respected.
formula_principle: Triangle law of addition: $\overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = \overrightarrow{AC}$.
common_misconception: The student subtracts the two sides instead of adding them, or reverses the order of the letters.

subtopic: Scalar multiplication of a vector
concept_tested: Effect of a negative scalar on the magnitude of a vector
stem: If $|\vec{a}| = 5$, then $|-4\vec{a}|$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student carries the sign of the scalar into the magnitude, which can never be negative.
distractor_rationale.C: The student believes scalar multiplication alters only the direction and leaves the magnitude unchanged.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides by the scalar instead of multiplying by its modulus.

solution: Scalar multiplication by $k$ scales the length by the factor $|k|$ and, when $k < 0$, reverses the direction. Here $k = -4$, so $|-4\vec{a}| = |-4|\,|\vec{a}| = 4 \times 5 = 20$. The direction of $-4\vec{a}$ is opposite to that of $\vec{a}$, but a magnitude is a length and is never negative, so the answer is $20$ and not $-20$.
formula_principle: For any scalar $k$ and any vector $\vec{a}$, $|k\vec{a}| = |k|\,|\vec{a}|$.
common_misconception: The student lets the negative sign of the scalar pass into the magnitude.

subtopic: Scalar multiplication of a vector
concept_tested: Finding the scalar multiple with a prescribed magnitude and the opposite direction
stem: If $\vec{b}$ is a scalar multiple of $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ with $|\vec{b}| = 12$ and $\vec{b}$ oppositely directed to $\vec{a}$, then $\vec{b}$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student finds the right length but ignores the requirement that the direction be opposite.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the scalar $-12$ directly, without dividing by $|\vec{a}|$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides by $|\vec{a}|^{2}$ instead of $|\vec{a}|$ when finding the scalar.

solution: Write $\vec{b} = \lambda\vec{a}$. Since $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$, the condition $|\vec{b}| = 12$ gives $|\lambda| \times 3 = 12$, so $|\lambda| = 4$. concept_tested: Fourth vertex of a parallelogram using equality of vectors
stem: If A$(1, 2, -1)$, B$(3, 5, 5)$ and C$(6, 7, 8)$ are three vertices of a parallelogram ABCD, then the fourth vertex D is

distractor_rationale.A: The student adds $\overrightarrow{AB}$ to C instead of subtracting it, reversing the joining vector.

distractor_rationale.D: The student computes the midpoint of the diagonal AC and reports it as the vertex.

Now $\overrightarrow{AB} = (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (5 - 2)\hat{j} + (5 + 1)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. Writing $\overrightarrow{DC} = \vec{c} - \vec{d}$ gives $\vec{d} = \vec{c} - \overrightarrow{AB} = \left(6\hat{i} + 7\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}\right) - \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}\right) = 4\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, so D is $(4, 4, 2)$. As a check, $\overrightarrow{AD} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, so the other pair of sides is also parallel and equal.

subtopic: Collinearity of three points using vectors
concept_tested: Finding an unknown coordinate that makes three points collinear
stem: If the points A$(1, 2, 3)$, B$(3, 5, 9)$ and C$(k, 8, 15)$ are collinear, then $k$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student finds that the first component of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ is $4$ and reports it as the coordinate of C.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes $\overrightarrow{CA}$ in place of $\overrightarrow{AC}$ and solves $1 - k = 4$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student reports the scalar of proportionality instead of the required coordinate.

solution: Compute the two vectors from A. $\overrightarrow{AB} = (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (5 - 2)\hat{j} + (9 - 3)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = (k - 1)\hat{i} + (8 - 2)\hat{j} + (15 - 3)\hat{k} = (k - 1)\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 12\hat{k}$. Comparing the $\hat{i}$ components, $k - 1 = 2 \times 2 = 4$, so $k = 5$. The coordinate is $k$ itself, not the component $k - 1$.

subtopic: Collinearity of three points using vectors
concept_tested: Ratio in which a point divides the join of two collinear points given by position vectors
stem: Let $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$ be non-coplanar vectors and let P, Q, R have position vectors $-2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 5\vec{c}$, $\vec{a} + 2\vec{b} + 3\vec{c}$ and $7\vec{a} - \vec{c}$ respectively. Then Q divides PR in the ratio

distractor_rationale.A: The student interchanges $m$ and $n$ while reading off the ratio.
distractor_rationale.B: The student uses the scalar $3$ from $\overrightarrow{PR} = 3\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$ directly as the second part of the ratio.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the same scalar $3$ and also interchanges the two parts.

solution: Work with the coefficients of $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$, $\vec{c}$, which is legitimate because the three vectors are non-coplanar. Then $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \left(\vec{a} + 2\vec{b} + 3\vec{c}\right) - \left(-2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 5\vec{c}\right) = 3\vec{a} - \vec{b} - 2\vec{c}$, and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \left(7\vec{a} - \vec{c}\right) - \left(-2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 5\vec{c}\right) = 9\vec{a} - 3\vec{b} - 6\vec{c} = 3\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$. So the three points are collinear and $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \dfrac{1}{3}\overrightarrow{PR}$, which places Q one third of the way from P to R. Hence $PQ : QR = 1 : 2$. The same conclusion follows from the section formula, since $\dfrac{1 \cdot \left(7\vec{a} - \vec{c}\right) + 2 \cdot \left(-2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b} + 5\vec{c}\right)}{1 + 2} = \vec{a} + 2\vec{b} + 3\vec{c}$, the position vector of Q.
formula_principle: If $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \lambda\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ with $0 < \lambda < 1$, then Q divides PR internally in the ratio $\lambda : (1 - \lambda)$.
common_misconception: The student converts $\overrightarrow{PR} = 3\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$ into the ratio $1 : 3$ or $3 : 1$ instead of $1 : 2$.

subtopic: Collinearity of three points using vectors
concept_tested: Unknown scalar in a position vector that forces three points to be collinear
stem: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be non-collinear vectors. The points P, Q, R have position vectors $3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}$, $\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}$ and $-\vec{a} + 4\vec{b}$ respectively. If P, Q, R are collinear, then $\lambda$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student matches the coefficient of $\vec{b}$ in $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ with that in $\overrightarrow{PR}$ without the scalar factor.
distractor_rationale.B: The student inverts the scalar factor and uses $t = 2$ in place of $t = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student sets the coefficient of $\vec{b}$ in $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ equal to zero.

solution: Form the two vectors from P. $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \left(\vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}\right) - \left(3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\right) = -2\vec{a} + (\lambda + 2)\vec{b}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \left(-\vec{a} + 4\vec{b}\right) - \left(3\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}\right) = -4\vec{a} + 6\vec{b}$. Collinearity means $\overrightarrow{PQ} = t\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ for some scalar $t$, so $-2\vec{a} + (\lambda + 2)\vec{b} = -4t\,\vec{a} + 6t\,\vec{b}$. Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are non-collinear, the coefficients may be equated separately. From the $\vec{a}$ terms, $-2 = -4t$, so $t = \dfrac{1}{2}$. From the $\vec{b}$ terms, $\lambda + 2 = 6t = 3$, so $\lambda = 1$. Then $\overrightarrow{PQ} = -2\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}$, which is indeed half of $\overrightarrow{PR}$.
formula_principle: P, Q, R are collinear if and only if $\overrightarrow{PQ} = t\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ for some scalar $t$; when $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are non-collinear the coefficients of $\vec{a}$ and of $\vec{b}$ may be compared separately.
common_misconception: The student equates the coefficients of $\vec{b}$ directly and forgets that the same scalar factor must be used for both coefficients.

subtopic: Section formula, internal division
concept_tested: Statement of the section formula for internal division
stem: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are the position vectors of A and B, the position vector of the point P dividing segment AB internally in the ratio $m : n$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student interchanges $m$ and $n$, attaching $m$ to the nearer point A.
distractor_rationale.B: The student quotes the formula for external division.
distractor_rationale.D: The student quotes the external formula and also interchanges $m$ and $n$.

solution: Let P divide AB internally so that $AP : PB = m : n$. Then $n\,\overrightarrow{AP} = m\,\overrightarrow{PB}$, that is $n\left(\vec{p} - \vec{a}\right) = m\left(\vec{b} - \vec{p}\right)$. Expanding, $n\vec{p} - n\vec{a} = m\vec{b} - m\vec{p}$, so $(m + n)\vec{p} = m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}$ and $\vec{p} = \dfrac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n}$. The scalar $m$, which is the part of the ratio next to A, multiplies the far position vector $\vec{b}$, and the denominator is a sum for internal division. Putting $m = n = 1$ recovers the midpoint $\dfrac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{2}$, a useful check on the form.
formula_principle: For internal division in the ratio $m : n$, $\vec{p} = \dfrac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n}$, where $AP : PB = m : n$.
common_misconception: The student attaches $m$ to $\vec{a}$ instead of to $\vec{b}$, interchanging the two parts of the ratio.

concept_tested: Position vector of the point of external division in a given ratio
stem: The position vectors of A and B are $\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. The position vector of the point dividing AB externally in the ratio $3 : 1$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses the internal division formula.
distractor_rationale.B: The student interchanges $m$ and $n$ in the external formula.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes $m + n$ in the denominator of the external formula instead of $m - n$.

solution: Here $m = 3$, $n = 1$, $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 5\hat{k}$. Then $m\vec{b} - n\vec{a} = \left(9\hat{i} + 12\hat{j} + 15\hat{k}\right) - \left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right) = 8\hat{i} + 10\hat{j} + 16\hat{k}$, and $m - n = 2$. Dividing, $\vec{p} = 4\hat{i} + 5\hat{j} + 8\hat{k}$. The point lies outside the segment, beyond B, which is what external division in a ratio greater than one must give, and a check confirms $AP : PB = 3 : 1$ in magnitude, since $\overrightarrow{AP} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 9\hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{PB} = -\hat{i} - \hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$.
formula_principle: For external division in the ratio $m : n$, $\vec{p} = \dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$, $m \ne n$.
common_misconception: The student uses a plus sign in the numerator or in the denominator, turning external division into internal division.

subtopic: Section formula, external division, and the midpoint
concept_tested: Finding the second end point from the midpoint
stem: If M$(3, 1, 5)$ is the midpoint of segment AB and A is $(1, -2, 3)$, then B is

distractor_rationale.A: The student computes $\overrightarrow{AM}$ and reports it as the point B.
distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the coordinates of M and A instead of using $2\vec{m} - \vec{a}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student writes $2\vec{a} - \vec{m}$, reversing the roles of the midpoint and the end point.

solution: From $\vec{m} = \dfrac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{2}$, multiply by $2$ to get $2\vec{m} = \vec{a} + \vec{b}$, hence $\vec{b} = 2\vec{m} - \vec{a}$. Componentwise, the first coordinate is $2(3) - 1 = 5$, the second is $2(1) - (-2) = 4$ and the third is $2(5) - 3 = 7$. So B is $(5, 4, 7)$. Checking, the midpoint of $(1, -2, 3)$ and $(5, 4, 7)$ is $\left(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{-2 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{3 + 7}{2}\right) = (3, 1, 5)$, which is M.
formula_principle: The midpoint of AB has position vector $\vec{m} = \dfrac{\vec{a} + \vec{b}}{2}$, so $\vec{b} = 2\vec{m} - \vec{a}$.
common_misconception: The student reports the vector from A to the midpoint instead of the position vector of B.

subtopic: Section formula, external division, and the midpoint
concept_tested: External division in a ratio whose first part is smaller
stem: The point C divides segment AB externally in the ratio $2 : 5$. If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are the position vectors of A and B, the position vector of C is

distractor_rationale.B: The student writes the denominator as $n - m = 3$ but leaves the numerator unchanged, losing a sign.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the internal division formula.
distractor_rationale.D: The student interchanges $m$ and $n$ in the external formula.

solution: Take $m = 2$ and $n = 5$, so $\vec{c} = \dfrac{2\vec{b} - 5\vec{a}}{2 - 5} = \dfrac{2\vec{b} - 5\vec{a}}{-3}$. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $-1$ gives $\vec{c} = \dfrac{5\vec{a} - 2\vec{b}}{3}$. Since $m < n$, the denominator $m - n$ is negative, and forgetting to carry that sign through is the usual slip. As a check, take $\vec{a} = \vec{0}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i}$. Then $\vec{c} = -2\hat{i}$, which lies outside the segment on the far side of A, with $CA : CB = 2 : 5$ in magnitude, exactly as external division in the ratio $2 : 5$ requires.
formula_principle: For external division in the ratio $m : n$, $\vec{c} = \dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$.
common_misconception: The student loses the sign of the denominator $m - n$ when $m$ is smaller than $n$.

subtopic: Section formula, external division, and the midpoint
concept_tested: Comparing the points of internal and external division in the same ratio
stem: The points P and Q divide the segment AB internally and externally respectively in the same ratio $3 : 1$. If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are the position vectors of A and B, then $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student computes $\vec{p} - \vec{q}$, reversing the vector joining the two points.
distractor_rationale.B: The student takes the midpoint of AB as the point of internal division instead of the point dividing in $3 : 1$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student interchanges $m$ and $n$ in the external division formula.

solution: With $m = 3$ and $n = 1$, the internal point has position vector $\vec{p} = \dfrac{3\vec{b} + \vec{a}}{4}$ and the external point has $\vec{q} = \dfrac{3\vec{b} - \vec{a}}{2}$. Then $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \vec{q} - \vec{p} = \dfrac{3\vec{b} - \vec{a}}{2} - \dfrac{3\vec{b} + \vec{a}}{4} = \dfrac{2\left(3\vec{b} - \vec{a}\right) - \left(3\vec{b} + \vec{a}\right)}{4} = \dfrac{3\vec{b} - 3\vec{a}}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}\left(\vec{b} - \vec{a}\right)$. So $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is three quarters of $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and points the same way as $\overrightarrow{AB}$. The two denominators, $m + n$ and $m - n$, are different, and that is the step where the work usually goes wrong.
formula_principle: Internal division in $m : n$ gives $\dfrac{m\vec{b} + n\vec{a}}{m + n}$ and external division in $m : n$ gives $\dfrac{m\vec{b} - n\vec{a}}{m - n}$; also $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \vec{q} - \vec{p}$.
common_misconception: The student uses the same denominator for both points, or subtracts in the wrong order at the end.

subtopic: Direction cosines and direction ratios
concept_tested: Direction cosines of a vector given in component form
stem: The direction cosines of the vector $12\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ are

distractor_rationale.B: The student reports the direction ratios when the direction cosines are asked for.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the sum of the components instead of by the magnitude.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides the squares of the components by the square of the magnitude.

solution: The magnitude is $\sqrt{12^{2} + (-3)^{2} + 4^{2}} = \sqrt{144 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{169} = 13$. The direction cosines are the components of the unit vector along $\vec{r}$, so they are $\dfrac{12}{13}$, $-\dfrac{3}{13}$ and $\dfrac{4}{13}$. The numbers $12$, $-3$, $4$ are direction ratios, not direction cosines: direction ratios are any triple proportional to the components, while the direction cosines are the one particular proportional triple whose squares add up to $1$. Here $\dfrac{144}{169} + \dfrac{9}{169} + \dfrac{16}{169} = 1$, as it must be.
formula_principle: The direction cosines of $\vec{r} = a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}$ are the components of the unit vector $\dfrac{\vec{r}}{|\vec{r}|}$, that is $l = \dfrac{a}{|\vec{r}|}$, $m = \dfrac{b}{|\vec{r}|}$, $n = \dfrac{c}{|\vec{r}|}$.
common_misconception: The student quotes the direction ratios in place of the direction cosines.

subtopic: Direction cosines and direction ratios
concept_tested: Direction cosines of the line joining two points
stem: The direction cosines of the line joining A$(1, -1, 2)$ to B$(3, 2, 8)$ are

distractor_rationale.A: The student reports the direction ratios when the direction cosines are asked for.
distractor_rationale.B: The student subtracts the coordinates of B from those of A, reversing the vector joining the two points.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the sum of the direction ratios instead of by the magnitude.

solution: First $\overrightarrow{AB} = (3 - 1)\hat{i} + (2 + 1)\hat{j} + (8 - 2)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$, so the direction ratios of the line are $2$, $3$, $6$. Its magnitude is $\sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7$. Dividing each ratio by $7$ gives the direction cosines $\dfrac{2}{7}$, $\dfrac{3}{7}$, $\dfrac{6}{7}$. As a check, $\dfrac{4}{49} + \dfrac{9}{49} + \dfrac{36}{49} = 1$. Taking $\overrightarrow{BA}$ instead would give the direction cosines of the same line measured in the opposite sense, so the order of the points must be respected.
formula_principle: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \vec{b} - \vec{a}$ gives direction ratios, and dividing each by $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ gives the direction cosines.
common_misconception: The student stops at the direction ratios, or subtracts the coordinates in the wrong order.

subtopic: Direction cosines and direction ratios
concept_tested: Building a vector of given magnitude from given direction ratios
stem: A vector $\vec{r} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}$ has magnitude $15$ and has the same direction as the vector with direction ratios $1, -2, 2$. Then $x + y + z$ =

distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the direction ratios themselves, treating them as the components of $\vec{r}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student multiplies by the magnitude $3$ of the direction ratio vector instead of dividing by it, using $15 \times 3$ as the scale factor.
distractor_rationale.D: The student scales the direction ratios by $15$ without dividing by their magnitude.

solution: The vector with direction ratios $1, -2, 2$ is $\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$, of magnitude $\sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = 3$. Its unit vector is $\dfrac{1}{3}\left(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\right)$, and the direction cosines are $\dfrac{1}{3}$, $-\dfrac{2}{3}$, $\dfrac{2}{3}$. Multiplying the unit vector by the required magnitude $15$ gives $\vec{r} = 5\left(\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\right) = 5\hat{i} - 10\hat{j} + 10\hat{k}$. Hence $x + y + z = 5 - 10 + 10 = 5$. A check on the magnitude gives $\sqrt{25 + 100 + 100} = \sqrt{225} = 15$, as required. Direction ratios fix only the direction, so they must be scaled by $\dfrac{15}{3}$, not used as components.
formula_principle: If a vector has direction ratios $a, b, c$ and magnitude $k$, then $\vec{r} = \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}}\left(a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}\right)$.
common_misconception: The student uses the direction ratios directly as the components of the vector, ignoring the required magnitude.

subtopic: The identity that the squares of the direction cosines sum to one
concept_tested: Finding the third direction angle from two given angles
stem: A line makes an angle of $90^{\circ}$ with the x axis, $60^{\circ}$ with the y axis and an obtuse angle with the z axis. The angle it makes with the z axis is

distractor_rationale.A: The student solves for the acute angle and ignores the condition that the angle is obtuse.
distractor_rationale.C: The student subtracts the two given angles from $270^{\circ}$ instead of using the identity.
distractor_rationale.D: The student drops the $90^{\circ}$ term and solves $\cos^{2}\gamma = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

solution: Here $\alpha = 90^{\circ}$ and $\beta = 60^{\circ}$, so $\cos\alpha = 0$ and $\cos\beta = \dfrac{1}{2}$. The identity gives $0 + \dfrac{1}{4} + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$, so $\cos^{2}\gamma = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\cos\gamma = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Both signs are geometrically possible in general, but the angle with the z axis is stated to be obtuse, so $\cos\gamma$ is negative and $\cos\gamma = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, giving $\gamma = 150^{\circ}$. A check confirms $0 + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1$.
formula_principle: If a line makes angles $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ with the coordinate axes then $\cos^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\beta + \cos^{2}\gamma = 1$.
common_misconception: The student takes the positive square root automatically and reports the acute angle.

subtopic: The identity that the squares of the direction cosines sum to one
concept_tested: Testing whether a given triple can be a set of direction cosines
stem: Can $\dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{1}{2},\ \dfrac{1}{2}$ be the direction cosines of a line?

options.A: Yes, because each of the three numbers lies between $-1$ and $1$
options.C: Yes, because the three numbers are equal, so the line makes equal angles with the axes

distractor_rationale.A: The student checks only that a cosine must lie between $-1$ and $1$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes equal angles alone are enough and never tests the identity.
distractor_rationale.D: The student tests the sum of the direction cosines instead of the sum of their squares.

solution: Test the identity. Here $l^{2} + m^{2} + n^{2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, which is not $1$, so the triple cannot be a set of direction cosines. Each number does lie between $-1$ and $1$, but that is necessary and not sufficient. The triple $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}$ is a valid set of direction ratios, and the corresponding direction cosines are obtained by dividing each by $\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, which gives $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
formula_principle: A triple $l, m, n$ is a set of direction cosines if and only if $l^{2} + m^{2} + n^{2} = 1$.
common_misconception: The student tests the sum of the numbers, or only their size, instead of the sum of their squares.

subtopic: The identity that the squares of the direction cosines sum to one
concept_tested: Vector of given magnitude making equal acute angles with the three axes
stem: A vector of magnitude $6\sqrt{3}$ makes equal acute angles with the three coordinate axes. That vector is

distractor_rationale.A: The student treats $1, 1, 1$ as the direction cosines and scales them by the magnitude.
distractor_rationale.B: The student divides the magnitude by $3$ instead of by $\sqrt{3}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student multiplies the magnitude by $\sqrt{3}$ instead of dividing by it.

solution: Let the equal angles be $\alpha$, so $l = m = n = \cos\alpha$. The identity gives $3\cos^{2}\alpha = 1$, hence $\cos\alpha = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. The angles are acute, so $\cos\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and the unit vector along $\vec{r}$ is $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)$. Multiplying by the magnitude, $\vec{r} = 6\sqrt{3} \cdot \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) = 6\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) = 6\hat{i} + 6\hat{j} + 6\hat{k}$. Checking, $\sqrt{36 + 36 + 36} = \sqrt{108} = 6\sqrt{3}$, as required.
formula_principle: If the angles with the axes are equal then $l = m = n$, and $l^{2} + m^{2} + n^{2} = 1$ forces $l = m = n = \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$; the vector is then $|\vec{r}|\left(l\hat{i} + m\hat{j} + n\hat{k}\right)$.
common_misconception: The student uses the equal direction ratios $1, 1, 1$ as direction cosines and forgets the factor $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

subtopic: Linear combination of vectors, and expressing one vector in terms of others
concept_tested: Expressing a vector as a linear combination of two given vectors
stem: If $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$, $\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$ and $\vec{c} = 5\hat{i} + \hat{j}$, then $\vec{c}$ =

distractor_rationale.B: The student interchanges the two coefficients when solving the pair of equations.
distractor_rationale.C: The student makes a sign slip while eliminating and obtains a negative second coefficient.
distractor_rationale.D: The student interchanges the coefficients and also mishandles the sign.

solution: Put $\vec{c} = x\vec{a} + y\vec{b}$. Then $5\hat{i} + \hat{j} = x\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j}\right) + y\left(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right) = (x + y)\hat{i} + (x - y)\hat{j}$. Equating the coefficients of $\hat{i}$ gives $x + y = 5$, and equating those of $\hat{j}$ gives $x - y = 1$. Adding, $2x = 6$, so $x = 3$, and then $y = 2$. Hence $\vec{c} = 3\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}$. Checking, $3\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j}\right) + 2\left(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\right) = 5\hat{i} + \hat{j}$, which is $\vec{c}$.
formula_principle: To write $\vec{c} = x\vec{a} + y\vec{b}$, equate the coefficients of $\hat{i}$ and of $\hat{j}$ and solve the resulting equations for $x$ and $y$.
common_misconception: The student attaches the coefficients to the wrong vectors after solving the simultaneous equations.

subtopic: Linear combination of vectors, and expressing one vector in terms of others
concept_tested: Coefficients in a vanishing linear combination of non-collinear vectors
stem: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be non-collinear vectors. If $(x - 1)\vec{a} + (2y + 3)\vec{b} = \vec{0}$, then $x + y$ =

distractor_rationale.A: The student solves $2y + 3 = 0$ as $y = \dfrac{3}{2}$, dropping the negative sign.
distractor_rationale.B: The student solves $2y + 3 = 0$ as $y = -3$, forgetting to divide by $2$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student solves $x - 1 = 0$ as $x = -1$ and also drops the sign of $y$.

solution: Suppose $x - 1 \ne 0$. Then $\vec{a} = -\dfrac{2y + 3}{x - 1}\vec{b}$, which would make $\vec{a}$ a scalar multiple of $\vec{b}$ and hence collinear with it, contradicting the hypothesis. So $x - 1 = 0$, and then $(2y + 3)\vec{b} = \vec{0}$ with $\vec{b} \ne \vec{0}$ forces $2y + 3 = 0$. Therefore $x = 1$ and $y = -\dfrac{3}{2}$, so $x + y = 1 - \dfrac{3}{2} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. The whole strength of the question is the theorem that a vanishing linear combination of two non-collinear vectors must have both coefficients zero.
formula_principle: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are non-collinear and $p\vec{a} + q\vec{b} = \vec{0}$, then $p = 0$ and $q = 0$.
common_misconception: The student solves the linear equations carelessly, most often mishandling the sign or the factor $2$ in $2y + 3 = 0$.

subtopic: Linear combination of vectors, and expressing one vector in terms of others
concept_tested: Solving for two unknowns from a vector equation in non-collinear vectors
stem: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be non-collinear vectors, $\vec{p} = (x + 4y)\vec{a} + (2x + y + 1)\vec{b}$ and $\vec{q} = (y - 2x + 2)\vec{a} + (2x - 3y - 1)\vec{b}$. If $3\vec{p} = 2\vec{q}$, then

distractor_rationale.A: The student interchanges the two unknowns when writing down the solution.
distractor_rationale.C: The student drops the negative sign while solving $9y = -9$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student changes the sign of both unknowns after eliminating.

solution: Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are non-collinear, $3\vec{p} = 2\vec{q}$ may be split into two scalar equations. Comparing the coefficients of $\vec{a}$, $3(x + 4y) = 2(y - 2x + 2)$, that is $3x + 12y = 2y - 4x + 4$, so $7x + 10y = 4$. Comparing the coefficients of $\vec{b}$, $3(2x + y + 1) = 2(2x - 3y - 1)$, that is $6x + 3y + 3 = 4x - 6y - 2$, so $2x + 9y = -5$. Multiply the first equation by $9$ and the second by $10$ to get $63x + 90y = 36$ and $20x + 90y = -50$. Subtracting, $43x = 86$, so $x = 2$, and then $2(2) + 9y = -5$ gives $9y = -9$, so $y = -1$. Both equations check: $14 - 10 = 4$ and $4 - 9 = -5$.
formula_principle: For non-collinear $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, the equality of two linear combinations forces the coefficients of $\vec{a}$ and of $\vec{b}$ to be equal separately.
common_misconception: The student equates the whole vectors instead of the separate coefficients, or slips a sign when solving the pair of linear equations.

subtopic: Definition and geometric meaning of the scalar product
concept_tested: Statement of the definition of the scalar product of two vectors
stem: Let $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ be non-zero vectors inclined at an angle $\theta$, where $0^\circ \le \theta \le 180^\circ$. Then the scalar product $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is defined as

distractor_rationale.A: The student recalls the magnitude of the vector product and uses it as the scalar product.
distractor_rationale.C: The student remembers that a trigonometric ratio of the included angle appears but picks the wrong ratio.
distractor_rationale.D: The student divides the magnitudes instead of multiplying them, carrying over the shape of the projection formula.

solution: The scalar product, also called the dot product, of two non-zero vectors is the number $|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the two vectors when they are drawn from a common initial point. The result is a scalar, not a vector, which is why the operation carries that name. The factor $\cos\theta$ makes the product largest, namely $|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|$, when $\theta = 0^\circ$, zero when $\theta = 90^\circ$, and most negative when $\theta = 180^\circ$. The sine of the angle belongs to the vector product $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$, whose magnitude is $|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\sin\theta$.
formula_principle: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$.
common_misconception: The student interchanges the sine in the vector product with the cosine in the scalar product.

subtopic: Definition and geometric meaning of the scalar product
concept_tested: Reading the sign of the scalar product as information about the angle
stem: For non-zero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ it is given that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} < 0$. Then the angle $\theta$ between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ satisfies

distractor_rationale.A: The student associates a negative scalar product with an acute angle, ignoring the sign of the cosine.
distractor_rationale.B: The student confuses a negative scalar product with a zero scalar product.
distractor_rationale.C: The student assumes that only exactly opposite vectors can give a negative scalar product.

solution: Write $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. Both magnitudes are positive because the vectors are non-zero, so the sign of the scalar product is decided entirely by $\cos\theta$. Now $\cos\theta < 0$ exactly when $\theta$ lies between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. At $\theta = 90^\circ$ the cosine is zero and the scalar product vanishes, and for $\theta$ below $90^\circ$ the cosine is positive. Hence $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} < 0$ gives $90^\circ < \theta \le 180^\circ$, that is, the angle is obtuse or straight.
formula_principle: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$, and since $|\vec{a}| > 0$ and $|\vec{b}| > 0$, the sign of $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is the sign of $\cos\theta$.
common_misconception: The student treats the sign of the scalar product as carrying no information about the angle.

subtopic: Definition and geometric meaning of the scalar product
concept_tested: Geometric reading of the scalar product as a length times a projection
stem: For non-zero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, the number $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is equal to

options.A: $|\vec{b}|$ multiplied by the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$
options.B: $|\vec{a}|$ multiplied by the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$
options.C: the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ divided by $|\vec{b}|$
options.D: the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$

correct_answer_text: $|\vec{b}|$ multiplied by the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$

distractor_rationale.B: The student pairs the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ with the length of $\vec{a}$ rather than with the length of $\vec{b}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides by the length of $\vec{b}$ a second time, having already divided once inside the projection.
distractor_rationale.D: The student attaches the area interpretation, which belongs to the vector product, to the scalar product.

solution: Drop a perpendicular from the tip of $\vec{a}$ onto the line of $\vec{b}$. The signed length of the piece of that line cut off from the common initial point is $|\vec{a}|\cos\theta$, and this is precisely the scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$. Now $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta = |\vec{b}| \left(|\vec{a}|\cos\theta\right)$, so the scalar product is the length of $\vec{b}$ multiplied by the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$. Equivalently, dividing both sides by $|\vec{b}|$ gives the projection formula $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|} = |\vec{a}|\cos\theta$. The area of the parallelogram on $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\sin\theta$, which is the magnitude of the vector product and not the scalar product.
formula_principle: The scalar projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$, so $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{b}| \times \left(\text{scalar projection of } \vec{a} \text{ on } \vec{b}\right)$.
common_misconception: The student cannot separate the projection factor from the magnitude factor and multiplies the projection by the length of the wrong vector.

subtopic: Definition and geometric meaning of the scalar product
concept_tested: Evaluating a scalar product from the magnitudes and the included angle
stem: If $|\vec{a}| = 3$, $|\vec{b}| = 4$ and the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $60^\circ$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student multiplies the two magnitudes and drops the cosine factor altogether.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses $\sin 60^\circ$ in place of $\cos 60^\circ$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student takes the angle as the supplement $120^\circ$ and picks up a wrong sign.

solution: Here $|\vec{a}| = 3$, $|\vec{b}| = 4$ and $\theta = 60^\circ$, so $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3 \times 4 \times \cos 60^\circ$. Since $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$, this gives $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 12 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 6$. The answer is a pure number with no unit vectors in it, as it must be, because the scalar product of two vectors is a scalar. Note that $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$ while $\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so using the sine would give $6\sqrt{3}$, which is the magnitude of $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ and not the scalar product.
formula_principle: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$.
common_misconception: The student substitutes the sine of the included angle instead of the cosine.

subtopic: Scalar product in component form
concept_tested: Computing a scalar product directly from the components
stem: If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student mishandles the sign of the third product and writes $2 - 2 + 3$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student makes every component product positive before adding.
distractor_rationale.D: The student multiplies the three component products together instead of adding them.

solution: Multiply the corresponding components and add: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = (2)(1) + (-1)(2) + (3)(-1) = 2 - 2 - 3 = -3$. The component rule follows from $\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{k} = 1$ and $\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = \hat{j} \cdot \hat{k} = \hat{k} \cdot \hat{i} = 0$, so that all the cross terms in the expansion vanish. The signs of the components must be carried into the products, and the three products are added, never multiplied.
formula_principle: If $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = b_1\hat{i} + b_2\hat{j} + b_3\hat{k}$, then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3$.
common_misconception: The student loses a negative sign while multiplying corresponding components.

subtopic: Scalar product in component form
concept_tested: Scalar product of a sum of two vectors with a third vector, in components
stem: If $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{b} = -\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\vec{c} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j}$, then $(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c}$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student evaluates $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}$ alone and leaves out the contribution of $\vec{b}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student adds the components of $\vec{a} + \vec{b}$ instead of pairing them with the components of $\vec{c}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student evaluates $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$ alone and leaves out the contribution of $\vec{a}$.

solution: First add the vectors component by component: $\vec{a} + \vec{b} = (1 - 1)\hat{i} + (2 + 2)\hat{j} + (3 + 1)\hat{k} = 4\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$. Now take the scalar product with $\vec{c} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$: $(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c} = (0)(3) + (4)(1) + (4)(0) = 4$. The same answer follows from the distributive law: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} = 3 + 2 + 0 = 5$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c} = -3 + 2 + 0 = -1$, and $5 + (-1) = 4$. Remember to supply the missing $\hat{k}$ component of $\vec{c}$ as $0$.
formula_principle: $(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c} = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c} + \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}$, and in components $\vec{u} \cdot \vec{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + u_3v_3$.
common_misconception: The student forgets that a missing unit vector in a given vector means a zero component, or works with only one of the two vectors in the bracket.

subtopic: Scalar product in component form
concept_tested: Recovering a vector from its scalar products with given vectors
stem: A vector $\vec{a}$ satisfies $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{i} = 2$, $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{j} = -1$ and $\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 4$. Then $\vec{a}$ is

distractor_rationale.B: The student reads the third condition as giving the $\hat{k}$ component directly.
distractor_rationale.C: The student adds $2$ and subtracts nothing, using $4 + 2 - 1$ in place of $4 - 2 + 1$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student drops the negative sign carried by the second condition.

solution: Let $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$. Taking the scalar product with $\hat{i}$ picks out the first component, so $a_1 = 2$, and similarly $a_2 = -1$. The third condition gives $\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 4$, that is, $2 + (-1) + a_3 = 4$, so $a_3 = 3$. Hence $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. As a check, $\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = 2 - 1 + 3 = 4$, as required.
formula_principle: For $\vec{a} = a_1\hat{i} + a_2\hat{j} + a_3\hat{k}$, the scalar products with the unit vectors give $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{i} = a_1$, $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{j} = a_2$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \hat{k} = a_3$.
common_misconception: The student treats the scalar product with $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ as though it gave a single component rather than the sum of the three components.

subtopic: Scalar product in component form
concept_tested: Scalar product of a vector making equal angles with the axes
stem: A vector $\vec{a}$ of magnitude $3$ makes equal acute angles with all three coordinate axes. Then $\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student takes each component of $\vec{a}$ to be the whole magnitude $3$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ itself as $\vec{a}$, forgetting that its magnitude is $\sqrt{3}$ and not $3$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the unit vector along $\vec{a}$ in place of $\vec{a}$ and ignores the magnitude $3$.

solution: Since $\vec{a}$ makes equal acute angles with the three axes, its three components are equal and positive, so write $\vec{a} = t\hat{i} + t\hat{j} + t\hat{k}$ with $t > 0$. Then $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{t^2 + t^2 + t^2} = t\sqrt{3}$. Given $|\vec{a}| = 3$, we get $t\sqrt{3} = 3$, so $t = \sqrt{3}$ and $\vec{a} = \sqrt{3}\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)$. Hence $\vec{a} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3} = 3\sqrt{3}$. The same value comes from the definition, since the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ is $0^\circ$ and the product of the magnitudes is $3 \times \sqrt{3}$.
formula_principle: If a vector makes equal angles with the axes, its components are equal, and $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$.
common_misconception: The student sets each component equal to the magnitude instead of solving $t\sqrt{3} = 3$ for the common component.

subtopic: Angle between two vectors from the scalar product
concept_tested: Angle from the magnitudes and the scalar product
stem: If $|\vec{a}| = 2$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3$, then the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|}$ instead of $\cos\theta$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student divides by $|\vec{a}| + |\vec{b}|$ and then guesses the nearest standard angle.
distractor_rationale.D: The student concludes that the vectors are perpendicular without checking whether the scalar product is zero.

solution: Substitute in the formula for the angle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{3}{2 \times 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Since $\theta$ lies in $[0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}$, we get $\theta = 60^\circ$. The denominator must be the product of the two magnitudes; using only one of them, or their sum, destroys the result.
formula_principle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|}$.
common_misconception: The student uses the sine ratio in the angle formula instead of the cosine ratio.

subtopic: Angle between two vectors from the scalar product
concept_tested: Angle between two vectors given in component form
stem: The angle between the vectors $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student divides $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ by $|\vec{a}|$ alone and forgets $|\vec{b}|$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student equates $\sin\theta$ rather than $\cos\theta$ to $\dfrac{1}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student carries a wrong sign into the numerator and takes $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

solution: Write the vectors with all three components: $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 0\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 0\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. Then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = (1)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(1) = 1$, while $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 0} = \sqrt{2}$ and $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{0 + 1 + 1} = \sqrt{2}$. Hence $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$. Both magnitudes must appear in the denominator, since the formula divides by the product of the two lengths.
formula_principle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|}$, with $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ and the magnitudes computed from components.
common_misconception: The student divides the scalar product by only one of the two magnitudes.

concept_tested: Angle between vectors with unequal magnitudes in component form
stem: The angle between $\vec{a} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + \hat{k}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student writes $|\vec{b}|^{2} = 2$ in the denominator instead of $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{2}$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student divides $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ by $|\vec{a}|$ only, gets $1$, and concludes that the vectors are parallel.

formula_principle: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|}$.
common_misconception: The student uses the square of a magnitude in place of the magnitude itself in the denominator.

subtopic: Angle between two vectors from the scalar product
concept_tested: Angle recovered from the magnitude of the sum of two unit vectors
stem: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are unit vectors with $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = \sqrt{3}$, then the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is

distractor_rationale.A: The student equates $2\cos\theta$ to $\sqrt{3}$ and reads $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student assumes $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^{2} = |\vec{a}|^{2} + |\vec{b}|^{2}$ for every pair of vectors.
distractor_rationale.D: The student expands $|\vec{a} - \vec{b}|^{2}$ by mistake and obtains $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

solution: Square the given magnitude and expand the scalar product: $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^{2} = |\vec{a}|^{2} + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^{2}$. Since $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are unit vectors, $|\vec{a}|^{2} = |\vec{b}|^{2} = 1$, and $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^{2} = \left(\sqrt{3}\right)^{2} = 3$. Hence $3 = 1 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + 1$, giving $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \dfrac{1}{2}$. Now $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|} = \dfrac{1/2}{1 \times 1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta = 60^\circ$. The middle term $2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is exactly what makes the parallelogram law differ from the theorem of Pythagoras.
formula_principle: $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^{2} = (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = |\vec{a}|^{2} + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^{2}$.
common_misconception: The student drops the cross term $2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ when squaring the magnitude of a sum of vectors.

subtopic: Condition for two vectors to be perpendicular
concept_tested: Statement of the condition for perpendicularity of two non-zero vectors
stem: Two non-zero vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are perpendicular to each other if and only if

distractor_rationale.A: The student quotes the condition for parallel vectors in place of the condition for perpendicular vectors.
distractor_rationale.B: The student writes the condition for vectors in the same direction, where $\cos\theta = 1$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student confuses the vanishing of the scalar product with the value $1$ taken by $\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i}$.

solution: By definition $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta$. As the vectors are non-zero, $|\vec{a}| \ne 0$ and $|\vec{b}| \ne 0$, so the product vanishes exactly when $\cos\theta = 0$. For $\theta$ in $[0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ this happens only at $\theta = 90^\circ$. Hence the scalar product being zero is equivalent to the two vectors being perpendicular. The vanishing of the vector product $\vec{a} \times \vec{b}$ is the opposite situation, $\sin\theta = 0$, which describes parallel vectors.
formula_principle: For non-zero $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, $\vec{a} \perp \vec{b} \iff \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$.

subtopic: Condition for two vectors to be perpendicular
concept_tested: Testing several pairs of vectors for perpendicularity
stem: Which one of the following pairs of vectors is a pair of mutually perpendicular vectors?

distractor_rationale.B: The student stops after the first two component products and does not check the sum.
distractor_rationale.C: The student judges by the fact that no unit vector appears with the same sign in both vectors.

e 0$. For $3\hat{i} + \hat{j}$ and $\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ it is $3 - 2 + 0 = 1 
e 0$. For $\hat{i} - \hat{j}$ and $\hat{j} - \hat{k}$ it is $0 - 1 + 0 = -1 
e 0$. Only the first pair gives zero.

subtopic: Condition for two vectors to be perpendicular
concept_tested: Deducing perpendicularity from equal magnitudes of the sum and the difference
stem: If $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are non-zero vectors such that $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}| = |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|$, then

distractor_rationale.C: The student cancels the magnitude signs and concludes that the vectors are equal.

solution: Square both sides of the given equality, which is legitimate as magnitudes are non-negative. Then $|\vec{a} + \vec{b}|^{2} = |\vec{a} - \vec{b}|^{2}$ becomes $|\vec{a}|^{2} + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^{2} = |\vec{a}|^{2} - 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + |\vec{b}|^{2}$. Cancelling $|\vec{a}|^{2}$ and $|\vec{b}|^{2}$ from both sides leaves $4\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$, so $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$. As both vectors are non-zero, they are perpendicular. Geometrically the two sides of the equation are the diagonals of the parallelogram built on $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, and equal diagonals mean the parallelogram is a rectangle.

stem: $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are unit vectors such that $\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}$ is perpendicular to $5\vec{a} - 4\vec{b}$. Then $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ equals

solution: Perpendicularity gives $(\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}) \cdot (5\vec{a} - 4\vec{b}) = 0$. Since the scalar product is commutative, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$, and the two middle terms combine to $6\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$. Because $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ are unit vectors, $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = 1$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b} = 1$. The equation becomes $5 - 8 + 6\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$, that is, $6\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 3$, so $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

subtopic: Projection of one vector on another
concept_tested: Comparing the projection of a on b with the projection of b on a
stem: Let $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = 3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$. If $p$ is the projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ and $q$ is the projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}$, then $p : q$ equals

distractor_rationale.B: The student divides by $|\vec{a}|$ when projecting $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$, which inverts the ratio.
distractor_rationale.C: The student argues that since $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ the two projections must be equal.
distractor_rationale.D: The student uses the squares of the magnitudes in the denominators.

solution: Compute $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = (2)(3) + (-1)(-6) + (2)(2) = 6 + 6 + 4 = 16$. The magnitudes are $|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3$ and $|\vec{b}| = \sqrt{9 + 36 + 4} = 7$. Then $p = \dfrac{16}{7}$ and $q = \dfrac{16}{3}$, so $p : q = \dfrac{16}{7} : \dfrac{16}{3} = \dfrac{1}{7} : \dfrac{1}{3} = 3 : 7$. In general the common factor $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ cancels and the ratio of the two projections is $|\vec{a}| : |\vec{b}|$. The scalar product is commutative, but the projection is not symmetric, because the two projections are divided by different magnitudes.
formula_principle: Projection of $\vec{a}$ on $\vec{b}$ is $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$ and projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\vec{a}$ is $\dfrac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}|}$, so their ratio is $|\vec{a}| : |\vec{b}|$.
common_misconception: The student believes that the projection of one vector on another is a symmetric quantity because the scalar product is commutative.

stem: For all vectors $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$, which one of the following statements is correct?

distractor_rationale.A: The student uses the special case $\theta = 0^\circ$ as though it held for every pair of vectors.
distractor_rationale.B: The student interchanges the perpendicular and parallel conditions for a zero scalar product.
distractor_rationale.C: The student carries the anticommutative behaviour of the vector product across to the scalar product.

solution: The angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is the same as the angle between $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}$, and the multiplication of the two magnitudes is ordinary multiplication of real numbers, which is commutative. Hence $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$ always. In component form the same fact reads $a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3 = b_1a_1 + b_2a_2 + b_3a_3$. It is the vector product that changes sign under interchange, $\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\,\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$. Perpendicular non-zero vectors have scalar product $0$, whereas parallel non-zero vectors have scalar product equal to the product of their magnitudes up to sign.
formula_principle: $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos\theta = |\vec{b}|\,|\vec{a}|\cos\theta = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$.
common_misconception: The student carries the anticommutative rule of the vector product over to the scalar product.

subtopic: Properties of the scalar product: commutative, distributive, not associative
concept_tested: Distributive law holds while an associative law cannot even be stated
stem: For all vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$, which one of the following statements is correct?

distractor_rationale.A: The student assumes an associative law by analogy with the multiplication of numbers, without noticing that $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is a scalar and cannot be dotted with a vector.
distractor_rationale.C: The student shifts the bracket from one vector to another as though addition and the scalar product could be exchanged freely.
distractor_rationale.D: The student ignores the factor $|\cos\theta|$, which equals $1$ only for parallel vectors.

solution: The distributive law is proved from the component form: the $r$th component of $\vec{b} + \vec{c}$ is $b_r + c_r$, so $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \sum a_r(b_r + c_r) = \sum a_rb_r + \sum a_rc_r = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}$. An associative law, on the other hand, cannot even be written down. The bracket $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$ is a scalar, and the scalar product is an operation between two vectors, so the symbol $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c}$ has no meaning at all. The same objection applies to $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c})$. What is meaningful is the vector $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})\vec{c}$, a scalar multiple of $\vec{c}$, and in general $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})\vec{c} \ne \vec{a}(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c})$, since the first is along $\vec{c}$ and the second along $\vec{a}$. Finally, $|\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}| = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}||\cos\theta| \le |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|$, with equality only for parallel vectors.
formula_principle: The scalar product is distributive over vector addition, $\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}$, but no associative law exists for it.
common_misconception: The student believes that the scalar product is associative, without seeing that the expression $(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c}$ is not even defined.

subtopic: Properties of the scalar product: commutative, distributive, not associative
concept_tested: Expanding a product of two linear combinations using the distributive law
stem: If $|\vec{a}| = 2$, $|\vec{b}| = 3$ and the angle between $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{b}$ is $60^\circ$, then $(2\vec{a} - \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} + 3\vec{b})$ equals

distractor_rationale.A: The student gives both middle terms a negative sign instead of combining them as $+5\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$.
distractor_rationale.B: The student multiplies only the like terms and leaves out the two cross terms.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}| = 6$ and forgets the factor $\cos 60^\circ$.

solution: First $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}|\,|\vec{b}|\cos 60^\circ = 2 \times 3 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 3$. Now expand: $(2\vec{a} - \vec{b}) \cdot (\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}) = 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} + 6\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} - \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} - 3\,\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}$. Using commutativity the middle terms combine to $5\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}$. Then $2|\vec{a}|^{2} + 5\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} - 3|\vec{b}|^{2} = 2(4) + 5(3) - 3(9) = 8 + 15 - 27 = -4$.
formula_principle: $(\alpha\vec{a} + \beta\vec{b}) \cdot (\lambda\vec{a} + \mu\vec{b})$ is expanded by the distributive law, using $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^{2}$, $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{b}|^{2}$ and $\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$.
common_misconception: The student mishandles the signs of the two cross terms while expanding the brackets.

subtopic: Work done as a scalar product, and other applications
concept_tested: Work done by a constant force through a displacement given by two points
stem: A constant force $\vec{F} = 3\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 5\hat{k}$ moves a particle from the point $A(1, 2, 3)$ to the point $B(4, 3, 1)$. The work done by the force, in the same system of units, is

distractor_rationale.B: The student writes the displacement as the position vector of $A$ minus that of $B$.
distractor_rationale.C: The student uses the position vector of $B$ as the displacement and ignores the starting point.
distractor_rationale.D: The student adds the two position vectors instead of subtracting them.

solution: The displacement is $\vec{d} = \overrightarrow{AB} = (4 - 1)\hat{i} + (3 - 2)\hat{j} + (1 - 3)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} - 2\hat{k}$. The work done by a constant force is the scalar product of the force and the displacement, so $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = (3)(3) + (2)(1) + (-5)(-2) = 9 + 2 + 10 = 21$. Work is a scalar, so no unit vectors appear in the answer. The order of subtraction matters: reversing it would reverse the sign of the work.
formula_principle: Work done $= \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$, where $\vec{d} = \overrightarrow{AB}$ is the displacement.
common_misconception: The student subtracts the position vectors in the wrong order, or uses a position vector in place of the displacement.

subtopic: Work done as a scalar product, and other applications
concept_tested: Work done from the magnitudes of the force and the displacement and the angle between them
stem: A force of magnitude $10$ units acts at $60^\circ$ to a displacement of magnitude $4$ units. The work done by the force, in the same system of units, is

distractor_rationale.A: The student multiplies the two magnitudes and leaves out the cosine of the angle.
distractor_rationale.B: The student uses $\sin 60^\circ$ in place of $\cos 60^\circ$.
distractor_rationale.D: The student multiplies the force by $\cos 60^\circ$ but forgets to multiply by the displacement.

solution: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work, and that component has magnitude $|\vec{F}|\cos\theta$. Hence $W = |\vec{F}|\,|\vec{d}|\cos\theta = 10 \times 4 \times \cos 60^\circ = 40 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 20$. If the force acted at right angles to the displacement, the cosine would be zero and no work would be done, which is why the cosine factor cannot be dropped.
formula_principle: Work done $= \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = |\vec{F}|\,|\vec{d}|\cos\theta$.
common_misconception: The student multiplies the magnitudes of force and displacement without resolving the force along the displacement.

subtopic: Work done as a scalar product, and other applications
concept_tested: Total work done by two forces acting together on a particle
stem: Two forces $\vec{F_1} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{F_2} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ act at the same point of a particle which moves from $A(2, 1, -1)$ to $B(3, -1, 2)$. The total work done, in the same system of units, is

distractor_rationale.B: The student computes the work done by the first force only.
distractor_rationale.C: The student computes the work done by the second force only.
distractor_rationale.D: The student takes the displacement from $B$ to $A$ instead of from $A$ to $B$.

solution: The resultant force is $\vec{F_1} + \vec{F_2} = (1 + 2)\hat{i} + (2 - 1)\hat{j} + (-3 + 4)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}$. The displacement is $\vec{d} = \overrightarrow{AB} = (3 - 2)\hat{i} + (-1 - 1)\hat{j} + (2 + 1)\hat{k} = \hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$. Hence the total work is $\left(\vec{F_1} + \vec{F_2}\right) \cdot \vec{d} = (3)(1) + (1)(-2) + (1)(3) = 3 - 2 + 3 = 4$. Working force by force gives the same total, since $\vec{F_1} \cdot \vec{d} = 1 - 4 - 9 = -12$ and $\vec{F_2} \cdot \vec{d} = 2 + 2 + 12 = 16$, and $-12 + 16 = 4$. This equality is exactly the distributive law for the scalar product.
formula_principle: For forces acting at the same point, the total work is $\left(\vec{F_1} + \vec{F_2}\right) \cdot \vec{d}$, which by the distributive law equals $\vec{F_1} \cdot \vec{d} + \vec{F_2} \cdot \vec{d}$.
common_misconception: The student adds only one of the two forces, or reverses the direction of the displacement.
